items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: I always felt that the earliest books of Robert Goffin’s book in Belgium were rather skimpy and he was writing as an enthusiast

ctx.x: Yes certainly it was before LPs, but the idea of him spreading through recording.

Well that’s absolutely true, because people got to know the history of jazz that way, through LPs even more than those 78s that I just talked about, that started around 1940. And the fact that it was an organized series meant that people knew that they could expect another release the following month, and that way they were on the lookout. And the annotations that I wrote for the 78 RPM albums were the first group of written documentation of the careers of some of these performers, because before that there…

rather special reason that I didn’t catch on to at first, which was that the American jazz records that got released abroad tended to stay in the catalogues. They didn’t sell very widely and the record business was smaller in Europe than it was in America, and because they stayed in the catalogues they were there for reference as more and more people got interested in the historical recordings of the 1920s and early 30s. items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: the very first book on jazz was written by a Belgian, Robert Goffin, and the second book, which was substantially better, was written by Hughes Panassié.

ctx.x: Bill Russell – I hope that somebody writes a book about him. I don’t know who’s going to do it. Bill Russell was a classically trained violinist who became, or tried to become, a contemporary classical composer. I don’t know how much he wrote, but he went into a branch, which we’ll get into in a second, which was extraordinary. His name was Russell Wagner. He changed his name to William Russell because he didn’t want to sign his scores “R. Wagner.” Bill turned to something which he was inspired to do by…

Juilliard to perform a Russian concerto at a program at the Juilliard School put on for Russian war relief, she had the very interesting idea of not performing the Tchaikovsky or Rachmaninoff or Prokofiev concertos, one of them, but instead find a new composer who was more representative of the spirit of that program, which was to solidify the Soviet and American fight against Fascism and Hitler. She came across the name Khachaturian, looked up the concerto, and saw, wow, it’s really fine. He’s Armenian. Great.…
